chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: ten thousand and the new TTh column first, then reading, writing, patterns, comparing and ordering, the number line and rounding, and finally the journeys and puzzles that use large numbers. Every idea starts with something the student does, and the tools put number cards, tokens and number lines in the student's hands.

points.title: Build it, then name it
points.text: Students first build a number from tokens or cards and only then read it, write it in digits with commas and write its name. The chart shows where every digit sits.

points.title: Predict before the reveal
points.text: Each idea opens with a question answered before the picture: what comes after nine thousand, which of two numbers is greater, which ten is nearest to 2,346.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: an odometer, ten-thousand builder, token table, pattern rule finder, compare chart, number line, rabbit rounder, vehicle loader, digit difference machine and the king's stable. Ideas about meaning and puzzles that need only a discussion carry no tool.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Each Let Us Do, Let Us Think and puzzle question is its own short video, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

modules.module_name: Big Numbers: Reading, Writing and Comparing
modules.module_summary: Counting thousands up to ten thousand, the new Ten Thousands column, reading and writing five-digit numbers with commas and number names, patterns in sequences, comparing and ordering large numbers, placing them on a number line, swapping digits, expanded form and counting in tens, hundreds and thousands.

concepts.concept_name: How far did you go on your last trip?

content.text:
When was the last time you went on a long trip? Where did you go? How did you travel? What was the duration of your trip? How much distance did you cover? Ask the elders who went with you to help you answer these questions.
Human beings have always been interested in travelling. About a hundred years ago, there were far fewer vehicles than today. There were animal-drawn carts, cars, and trains. Long before this, thousands of years ago, people travelled long distances on foot or used animals to travel from one place to another. They also built boats and ships to travel across lakes, rivers, and seas. Boats were probably the first form of transport invented by humans, much before bullock carts! Do you know how many vehicles are currently there in your state?

concepts.concept_name: Try it: read the odometer

content.text:
An odometer shows how many kilometres a vehicle has covered.
Each wheel of the odometer is one place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and now ten thousands.
When the ones wheel passes 9 it turns back to 0 and moves the next wheel by one.

student_does: Press Drive and watch the wheels turn from 0 up.
Choose a step of 1, 10, 100 or 1,000 and press Drive again.
Turn any wheel by hand to make a number you are asked for.
Read the number under the wheels and say it aloud.
challenges: Drive the bus from 0 to 999 and watch the wheels; what happens to the tens wheel?
Add 1 to 999. What do the three wheels do?
Drive in steps of 1,000 from 0 until the wheels cannot show the number in four places.

Set it to read 12,214.

concepts.concept_name: What comes after nine thousand?

content.text:
How do you write numbers to show several thousand objects?
Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
1,000 2,000 ... 9,000
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

Let us start with 1,000. What numbers do we get when we keep adding a thousand?
What number do we get when we add a thousand to 9,000? We get ten thousand. How do we write this number?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if you keep adding a thousand to 1,000, which number comes after 9,000?
2. 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, and so on up to 9,000. Each step adds one more thousand.
3. 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000. Ten thousands make ten thousand, and the number needs a new place.

content.text:
Worked example: Keep adding a thousand to 1,000. Which number do you reach after 9,000, and how many thousands is it?
1. 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, 6,000, 7,000, 8,000, 9,000.
2. One more thousand: 9,000 + 1,000 = 10,000.
3. 10,000 is 10 thousands, called ten thousand.
Answer: 10,000, which is ten thousand and is 10 thousands

concepts.concept_name: The new TTh column

content.text:
Look at the table below and notice the pattern of writing numbers. In the place value chart, we have added another column, TTh. It stands for ten thousand.
10 Ones = 1 Ten = 10, 10 Tens = 1 Hundred = 100, 10 Hundreds = 1 Thousand = 1,000.
In the same way, 10 Thousands = Ten Thousand = 10,000.
We use a comma to help us read large numbers easily.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the chart has columns for ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Where will 10 thousands go?
2. Ten of one place always make one of the next place to the left: 10 ones, 10 tens, 10 hundreds, 10 thousands.
3. So 10 thousands make 1 in a new column, TTh, with zeros in the four places to its right: 10,000.
4. The comma sits after the thousands place and helps the eye read the number.

concepts.concept_name: Reading numbers in the Indian place value system

content.text:
Do you remember how we read and write numbers in the Indian place value system? We use the same ten digits 0 to 9 in different places to write larger numbers.
For example, 1,380 = 1 Thousand + 3 Hundreds + 8 Tens + 0 Ones.
9,123 = 9 Thousands + 1 Hundred + 2 Tens + 3 Ones.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students count in thousands up to 9,000 and say that adding one more thousand gives ten thousand.
Students extend the place value chart with a TTh column, state that 10 thousands is 1 ten thousand and that 10 tens, 10 hundreds and 10 thousands each make the next place, and write 10,000.
Students read and write a number as thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, such as 1,380 and 9,123, using the same ten digits in different places.
Students build numbers from ones to ten thousand by dropping tokens in the place value chart, watch ten tokens regroup into one of the next place, and read each number aloud.

concepts.concept_name: Numbers just after ten thousand

content.text:
Let us see how we write numbers beyond 10,000 and how we name them. We write them in the same way as numbers below 9,999. You can use the tokens given in the end of the book.
10,001: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 1: Ten thousand one.
10,002: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 0, O 2: Ten thousand two.
10,010: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 1, O 0: Ten thousand ten.
10,024: TTh 1, Th 0, H 0, T 2, O 4: Ten thousand twenty-four.

content.text:
1. Predict first: one 10,000 token and one 1 token, what number is it and how do we say it?
2. 10,000 + 1 = 10,001, said ten thousand one. The zeros hold the Th, H and T places.
3. The same idea works for 10,002, 10,010 and 10,024: the TTh digit stays 1 and only the small places change.

content.text:
Worked example: One 10,000 token with two 1 tokens, one 10,000 token with one 10 token, and one 10,000 token with two 10 tokens and four 1 tokens. Write each number and its name.
1. 10,000 + 2 = 10,002, Ten thousand two.
2. 10,000 + 10 = 10,010, Ten thousand ten.
3. 10,000 + 20 + 4 = 10,024, Ten thousand twenty-four.
Answer: 10,002 is ten thousand two, 10,010 is ten thousand ten and 10,024 is ten thousand twenty-four

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

media.generation_prompt: Five columns left to right with headers TTh, Th, H, T, O. Below that, the number 11,214 written large with the words 'Eleven thousand two hundred fourteen' under it.

concepts.concept_name: Adding the same number each time

content.text:
1. Predict first: 2,000, 2,500, 3,000. What do you add to get from one number to the next?
2. Subtract each number from the one after it: 2,500 − 2,000 = 500 and 3,000 − 2,500 = 500.
3. The change is the same each time, 500, so the rule is add 500. The next numbers are 3,500, 4,000 and 4,500.

content.text:

tool_config.title: Pattern Rule Finder: What Is the Jump?
tool_config.idea: A pattern of numbers has a rule. Jumping from one number to the next on a number line shows how much is added or taken away each time, and the same jump gives the next numbers.
tool_config.screen: A row of number cards with blanks, a number line that shows an arrow for each jump, a jump-size dial, and a Test the rule button that fills the blanks with the chosen jump.
student_does: Look at two neighbouring cards and drag the dial to the jump between them.
Press Test the rule and watch the arrow jumps fill the blanks.
Check that every card in the row now follows the rule.
Change the rule and see which cards no longer fit.
challenges: Sequence 456, 567, 678: find the jump and fill four blanks.
Sequence 1,050, blank, 3,150, 4,200: find the jump and the missing card.
Sequence 5,501, 6,401, 7,301: find the jump and fill two blanks.
Sequence 10,100, 10,200, 10,300 continuing to 10,900.
Sequence 10,992, 10,993: find the jump.
Sequence 73,005, 72,004: is the rule add or subtract, and how much?
feedback: Each correct jump draws an arrow in the colour of its rule; a wrong jump shows the two cards that do not match.
A blank filled by the rule turns green and keeps the arrow behind it.
A rule that adds when the cards fall is shown as an arrow pointing the wrong way.
tool_config.done_when: Every sequence is completed and the rule is named in words.

hint_ladder.text: How far apart are the first two cards?
Is the next card bigger or smaller than the one before?
Subtract the smaller neighbouring card from the bigger and try that jump on the next pair.
The jump between the first two cards is shown; test it on the third and fourth cards.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

concepts.concept_name: More digits, greater number

content.text:
1. Predict first: which is greater, 9,876 or 10,012?
2. Count the digits first. 9,876 has four digits and 10,012 has five digits.
3. A number with more digits is greater, because its leftmost digit sits in a bigger place. The size of the first digit does not matter when the digits are not equal in number.

concepts.concept_name: Same number of digits: compare from the left

content.text:
1. Predict first: 56,321 and 56,298 both have five digits. Which is greater, and which digit tells you?
2. Put both numbers on the place value chart, TTh Th H T O, one below the other.
3. Move from the left. TTh is 5 and 5, equal. Th is 6 and 6, equal. H is 3 and 2, different, so stop.
4. The number with the bigger digit at the first place where the digits differ is greater.

concepts.concept_name: Arranging numbers in order

content.text:
1. Predict first: to arrange 3,450, 34,500, 345 and 4,035 in increasing order, which one comes first?
2. Group by number of digits, then compare inside each group from the left.
3. Increasing means smaller to greater, ascending. Decreasing means greater to smaller, descending.
4. A number line also arranges numbers: the greater a number, the farther to the right.

Let Us Do 3, arrange in increasing order: Arrange in increasing order: 40,347, 34,407, 40,473, 34,740, 73,404, 74,430, 47,340 and 18,926.

4. With TTh digit 7: 73,404 and 74,430. Th is 3 and 4, so 73,404 is less than 74,430.

content.text:
Let Us Do 4, the student's claim: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 is greater than 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not?
1. 9,990 has 4 digits and 49,014 has 5 digits.
2. A number with more digits is greater, so 49,014 is greater.
3. The student compared 9 with 4 as if both numbers had the same number of digits.
Answer: The student is not correct: 9,990 < 49,014, because 49,014 has more digits

Answer: Sheetal's car, 67,543 km, has been driven more

Let Us Do (second set) 4, prices of electric bikes: Arrange the prices in ascending (increasing) order: 90,000, 89,999, 94,983, 49,900, 93,743 and 39,999.

3. So 90,000 is less than 93,743, which is less than 94,983.
Answer: 39,999, 49,900, 89,999, 90,000, 93,743, 94,983

So 90,000 is less than 93,743, which is less than 94,983.

content.text:
Let Us Do (second set) 5, population of towns: Arrange the populations in descending (decreasing) order: Town 1 65,232, Town 2 53,231, Town 3 56,380, Town 4 51,336, Town 5 45,858 and Town 6 66,540.
1. All have 5 digits. TTh is 6, 5, 5, 5, 4 and 6.
2. TTh 6: Town 6 (66,540) and Town 1 (65,232). Th is 6 and 5, so Town 6 is greater.
3. TTh 5: Town 3 (56,380), Town 2 (53,231) and Town 4 (51,336). Th is 6, 3 and 1.
4. Town 5 (45,858) has TTh 4, the smallest.
Answer: Town 6 (66,540), Town 1 (65,232), Town 3 (56,380), Town 2 (53,231), Town 4 (51,336), Town 5 (45,858)

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compare numbers with a different number of digits and say that the number with more digits is greater, whatever its first digit.
Students compare numbers with the same number of digits by looking at each place from the left on the place value chart, and stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Students arrange numbers in increasing (ascending) and decreasing (descending) order by sorting them by number of digits first and then comparing within each group.
Students compare and order numbers on the compare chart, with the digits in a place value chart and the numbers as markers on a number line.

final_answer.spoken: Town six with sixty-six thousand five hundred and forty, Town one with sixty-five thousand two hundred and thirty-two, Town three with fifty-six thousand three hundred and eighty, Town two with fifty-three thousand two hundred and thirty-one, Town four with fifty-one thousand three hundred and thirty-six and Town five with forty-five thousand eight hundred and fifty-eight

maths_rules: six towns: Town 1 65,232; Town 2 53,231; Town 3 56,380; Town 4 51,336; Town 5 45,858; Town 6 66,540; all have 5 digits
ten thousands digits: 6, 5, 5, 5, 4, 6; so the two with 6 come first, then the three with 5, then Town 5 with 4
Town 6 vs Town 1: thousands 6 and 5; 6 > 5, so 66,540 > 65,232
Town 3, Town 2, Town 4: thousands 6, 3, 1; so 56,380 > 53,231 > 51,336
slip: Town 5 has 8 in the hundreds place, but its ten thousands digit 4 is the smallest, so 45,858 is the least

concepts.concept_name: Where does a number sit on the line?

content.text:
1. Predict first: on a line marked 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000, where will 47,340 sit?
2. Find the two marks it lies between. 47,340 is more than 40,000 and less than 60,000.
3. Then look at how far it is from the nearer mark. It is only 7,340 past 40,000, so it sits closer to 40,000.
4. The greater the number, the farther to the right it is.

content.text:
Worked example: Between which two marks of 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000 does 47,340 sit, and which mark is it nearer to?
1. 47,340 is more than 40,000 and less than 60,000.
2. 47,340 − 40,000 = 7,340 and 60,000 − 47,340 = 12,660.
3. 7,340 is smaller than 12,660, so it is nearer to 40,000.
Answer: 47,340 sits between 40,000 and 60,000, nearer to 40,000

concepts.concept_name: Numbers between two numbers

content.text:
1. Predict first: name a number between 12,350 and 12,800. Is it the only one?
2. A number between them has to be greater than the first and less than the second. Keep the first digits the same and change the hundreds.
3. There are many such numbers. We can name some in steps of 100: 12,400, 12,500, 12,600 and 12,700.

concepts.concept_name: Digit swap

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 2,935, which two digits do you swap to get the largest number?
2. Swapping two digits changes two places at once. The place on the left matters more.
3. To make a number large, put the biggest digit in the leftmost place. To make it small, put the smallest digit there, if you can.

content.text:
Worked example: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the smallest number you can.
1. Largest: the biggest digit, 9, should be in the thousands place. Swap 2 and 9 to get 9,235.
2. Smallest: 2 is already the smallest digit, in the thousands place. Now put the next smallest, 3, in the hundreds place: swap 9 and 3 to get 2,395.
Answer: Largest 9,235 (swap 2 and 9), smallest 2,395 (swap 9 and 3)

tool_config.title: Number Line Placer: Where Does It Go?
tool_config.idea: A number line shows how far a number is from 0. Marking a number between two benchmark numbers by reading its place values tells us where on the line it sits.
tool_config.screen: A long number line with benchmark ticks at 0, 20,000, 40,000, 60,000 and 80,000, number cards to drag onto the line, a zoom bar that shows the line between two ticks in finer steps, and a ruler of place values under the chosen number.
student_does: Drag a number card to the place on the line where you think it belongs.
Zoom into the part of the line between two ticks to place it more exactly.
Press Check to see the number's true position and how far off the marker was.
Move the marker again until it sits on the number.
challenges: Place 40,347 and 40,473: which is to the right?

Place 73,404 and 74,430 between 60,000 and 80,000.
Place 47,340 and 18,926 and say which tick each is nearest to.
Place all eight numbers and read them from left to right.
Find a number between 23,568 and 24,234 and place it.
feedback: A correctly placed marker locks in with a tick mark and the number printed above.
A marker placed too far shows an arrow back towards the true place, never the exact spot.
When the line is zoomed, the ticks update to the new step and the cards already on the line stay.
tool_config.done_when: Every card is done with all markers on their true places.

hint_ladder.text: Between which two ticks does the number sit?
Look at the thousands and ten thousands digits to decide which two ticks.
Zoom into the stretch between those ticks and use the hundreds digit to place it.
Between 40,000 and 60,000, the number 47,340 sits just over a third of the way along.

tool_config.design_brief: Class 5 tool brief: interactive and doer-based, the student performs actions and does not only watch. The student can build and rearrange numbers, compare values, place markers on number lines, complete patterns and solve problems. Colourful, clear and engaging: number cards, place value tokens, number lines, arrows, visual counters and real-life travel illustrations, all of which can be selected, moved, changed or arranged. A simple uncluttered layout with one prominent main visual and only the controls that are needed. Immediate visual feedback: numbers update, markers move and correct arrangements are highlighted. Hints and feedback help the student discover the answer and never reveal it. Hands-on, visually engaging and conceptually clear.

media.title: Which two digits do you swap to get the biggest number?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Joseph swaps two digits of his bus ticket number. The video finds the swap that gives the largest number and the swap that gives the smallest.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the leftmost place is worth the most, so put the biggest digit there for the largest number. Watch for children who swap the two biggest digits.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says stop, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: Which two digits do you swap to get the biggest number?
items: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child knows place values but has not yet used them to choose which two digits to swap.

covers: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the

interaction_points.prompt: Swap two digits of six thousand, one hundred and eighty-four to make the largest and the smallest number.

source: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the
video_script.why: The child knows place values but has not yet used them to choose which two digits to swap.
video_script.substitution: Move the biggest digit into the leftmost place for the largest number, and keep or put the smallest digit there for the smallest.
video_script.anchor: Joseph's bus ticket number whose digits he may swap
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu swaps the two biggest digits, nine and five, and gets 2,539. The nine lands in the ones place and the thousands place still holds the small digit two.
video_script.payoff_line: the largest number is nine thousand, two hundred and thirty-five

final_answer.spoken: largest nine thousand two hundred and thirty-five by swapping two and nine, smallest two thousand three hundred and ninety-five by swapping nine and three

maths_rules: ticket 2,935: thousands 2, hundreds 9, tens 3, ones 5; the leftmost place is worth the most
slip: swap 9 and 5 gives 2,539, which is not the largest
largest: put 9, the biggest digit, in the thousands place; swap 2 and 9 to get 9,235
smallest: 2 is already the smallest digit and is in the thousands place; keep it; put 3, the next smallest, in the hundreds place; swap 9 and 3 to get 2,395
your turn: 6,184; largest swaps 6 and 8 to give 8,164; smallest swaps 6 and 1 to give 1,684; never shown
video_script.design: One idea: the leftmost place is worth the most, so it decides. Wrong idea: swap the two biggest digits. The ticket with four digit boxes stays on the stage.

media.title: Which five numbers are more than one and less than another?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Farhan draws raffle tickets at a school fair, and a winning ticket must lie between two limits. The video writes five winning numbers by choosing the hundreds.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a number more than one limit and less than the other must stay between both. Watch for a number that passes the low limit but is above the high limit.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

media.title: Which prices are whole thousands between two numbers?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Joseph's cycle shop sells cycles at whole-thousand prices. The video lists every price between two limits by finding the first and the last thousand.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: ones, tens and hundreds all zero means a whole number of thousands, so find the first and last thousand between the limits. Watch for a thousand just below the low limit.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

media.title: Which two digits can you swap to pass a target?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Kavya's lucky-draw ticket wins a prize if it is above a target after one swap. The video finds a swap that makes the thousands digit big enough.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: to pass a target, the leftmost place must be big enough, so bring a big digit to the front. Watch for a swap that leaves the thousands digit small.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

media.title: How do you swap digits to land in a range?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Tanvi's parcel number is changed by swapping two digits so it lands between two limits and then above a target. The video picks each swap by checking the front digits.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: choose the digit that goes into the leftmost place by looking at the range, then check. Watch for a swap that overshoots the upper limit.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do you swap digits to land in a range?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question
items: Let Us Do 5 (b), digit swap in 10,593
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can swap digits but has not yet chosen a swap to land inside a range or past a target.

covers: Let Us Do 5 (b), digit swap in 10,593

source: Let Us Do 5 (b), digit swap in 10,593
video_script.why: The child can swap digits but has not yet chosen a swap to land inside a range or past a target.
video_script.substitution: For a range, keep the front digit and choose a thousands digit that stays inside; for a target, bring a big enough digit to the front.
video_script.anchor: Tanvi's parcel number at the post office
video_script.wrong_answer: swap the zero and the nine
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu swaps the zero and the nine to make the thousands digit as big as possible and gets 19,503. That is above fifteen thousand, so it is outside the range.
video_script.payoff_line: the number becomes thirteen thousand, five hundred and ninety

final_answer.spoken: thirteen thousand five hundred and ninety, and fifty thousand one hundred and ninety-three

maths_rules: parcel 10,593 has digits 1, 0, 5, 9, 3: ten thousands 1, thousands 0
slip: swap 0 and 9 gives 19,503; 19,503 > 15,000, so it is outside the range
(i) between 11,000 and 15,000: the thousands digit must be 1 to 4 with 1 in front; swap 0 and 3 gives 13,590; 11,000 < 13,590 < 15,000
(ii) more than 35,000: the front digit must be 3 or more; swap 1 and 5 gives 50,193; 50,193 > 35,000
video_script.design: Exercise: two swaps with two targets. Hint: look at the front digits. The parcel with digit boxes stays on the stage.

media.title: How do you swap two digits to get the smallest number?
media.context: We the Travellers - I. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Harpreet's train ticket number is changed by one swap to the smallest and then the biggest number it can make. The video puts the smallest digit and then the biggest digit in front.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the front place decides, so bring the smallest digit there for the smallest number and the biggest digit there for the biggest. Watch for a swap that leaves the front digit unchanged.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do you swap two digits to get the smallest number?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question
items: Let Us Do 5 (c), digit swap in 48,247

source: Let Us Do 5 (c), digit swap in 48,247
video_script.why: The child knows the leftmost place matters most but has not yet chosen a swap for the smallest and the biggest number.
video_script.substitution: Swap the smallest digit into the front place for the smallest number, and the biggest digit into the front place for the biggest number.
video_script.anchor: Harpreet's train ticket number with five digits

final_answer.spoken: twenty-eight thousand four hundred and forty-seven, and eighty-four thousand two hundred and forty-seven

slip: swap 8 and 2 gives 42,847; the front digit is still 4; 42,847 > 28,447

biggest: the biggest digit is 8; swap the front 4 and the 8 to get 84,247

content.text:

2. 90 tens is 900. The remaining 83 are ones: 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones.

content.text:
Worked example: Write 983 as 90 Tens + __ Ones, and 4,560 as 45 Hundreds + __ Ones.
1. 90 Tens = 900, and 983 − 900 = 83, so 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones.
2. 45 Hundreds = 4,500, and 4,560 − 4,500 = 60, so 4,560 = 45 Hundreds + 60 Ones.
Answer: 983 = 90 Tens + 83 Ones and 4,560 = 45 Hundreds + 60 Ones

concepts.concept_name: How many notes?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many 10 rupee notes make 3,250 rupees?
2. 3 Tens is 30, 90 Tens is 900 and 700 Tens is 7,000. In 3,250, the number of tens is 325.
3. For hundreds, drop the last two digits: 32 hundreds are in 3,250. For thousands drop the last three: 3 thousands.
4. For 500 notes, count how many hundreds there are and divide by 5; the leftover is not enough for another note.

content.text:
Worked example: How many notes of 10, of 100, of 1,000 and of 500 are there in 3,250?
1. Notes of 10: 3,250 has 325 tens.
2. Notes of 100: 3,250 has 32 hundreds, with 50 left.
3. Notes of 1,000: 3,250 has 3 thousands, with 250 left.
4. Notes of 500: 32 hundreds is 5 hundreds six times with 2 hundreds over, so 6 notes of 500.
Answer: 325 notes of 10, 32 notes of 100, 3 notes of 1,000 and 6 notes of 500

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students write a number as the sum of the value of its digits, and use zero to hold an empty place.
Students write a number as tens plus ones, hundreds plus ones, and thousands plus hundreds plus tens plus ones, and see that there is more than one way.
Students tell how many notes of 10, 100, 500 or 1,000 make up a number by dividing the number into groups, and see that the leftover amount is not a full note.
Students write expanded forms and counts of tens, hundreds, thousands and notes for the numbers in the book's exercises.

media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; stop again at each hint and try once more.

video_script.why: The child knows tens and ones, but has not used take away to find a missing part of a number.
video_script.substitution: Take the given part from the whole number; the rest is the blank, regrouped as tens or ones.
video_script.anchor: Tanvi packing pencils into packets of ten at her uncle's stationery shop in Kolhapur
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu reads only the tens digit of sixty eight and writes six tens. Six tens and eighteen ones make seventy eight, not sixty eight.
video_script.payoff_line: take away what you are given

final_answer.spoken: five tens and two hundred and seven ones

maths_rules: slip: 6 Tens + 18 Ones = 60 + 18 = 78, not 68
video_script.design: Exercise. Hint: start from the whole number and take away the part given. The number 983, done in the book, sits on the board as packets and loose pencils.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='story'/>Tanvi packs pencils into packets of ten at her uncle's shop in Kolhapur.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Some blanks must be filled to say how many tens and ones a number has.

beats.on_screen: the items hold still and the anchor gets an accent underline

marks.stop: the anchor is underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud.

beats.on_screen: the done example: 983 shown as 90 packets of ten (900 pencils) and 83 loose pencils; a note says start from the whole number and take away the part you are given

marks.packs: 90 packets glow as 900, 83 loose pencils sit beside them

narration: <bookmark mark='done'/>Your book shows nine hundred and eighty three as ninety tens and eighty three ones.
<bookmark mark='packs'/>Ninety packets of ten hold nine hundred pencils, and eighty three pencils are loose.
<bookmark mark='hint'/>Start from the whole number, and take away the part you are given. Try again with this.

beats.on_screen: Chintu's bubble shows 68 = 6 Tens + 18 Ones; a sum 60 + 18 = 78 appears beside 68 and the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.chintu: Chintu's bubble appears with the wrong blank
marks.strike: the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='chintu'/>The six in sixty eight is the tens digit, so the blank is six tens.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Six tens is sixty, and sixty plus eighteen is seventy eight.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>That is more than sixty eight, so six tens cannot be right.

beats.on_screen: the rule line appears; the board shows 68 − 18 = 50 and then 50 = 5 Tens

marks.rule: the rule line appears
marks.tens: 50 regroups into 5 Tens and the blank shows 5 Tens

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Take away what you are given, and what is left fills the blank.
<bookmark mark='sub'/>Sixty eight take away eighteen leaves fifty.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>Fifty is five tens, because each ten holds ten ones.

beats.on_screen: the board shows 4 Hundreds = 400, then 607 − 400 = 207, and the blank shows 207 Ones
narration: <bookmark mark='hund'/>Four hundreds is four hundred.
<bookmark mark='sub'/>Six hundred and seven take away four hundred leaves two hundred and seven.
<bookmark mark='ones'/>The blank is two hundred and seven ones, because the hundreds are already counted.

beats.on_screen: two checks side by side: 50 + 18 = 68 and 400 + 207 = 607

marks.check: the words add the two parts appear
marks.one: the line 50 + 18 = 68 appears
marks.two: the line 400 + 207 = 607 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>To check, add the two parts and see if they make the whole number.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Fifty plus eighteen makes sixty eight.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Four hundred plus two hundred and seven makes six hundred and seven.

media.description: Kavya's uncle stacks bricks near Mysuru. The video fills four place value splits by taking the given parts away from the whole number.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: add the parts given, take them from the whole, and share what is left among the blanks. Watch for a child who copies the digit of a place instead of counting all the units there.

interaction_points.answer: (d) 16 Hundreds and 1 Ones; (e) 5 Thousand and 69 Ones; (f) 2 Ten Thousand and 6 Hundreds; (g) 13 Thousand and 0 Hundreds

final_answer.value: (d) 16 Hundreds and 1 Ones; (e) 5 Thousand and 69 Ones; (f) 2 Ten Thousand and 6 Hundreds; (g) 13 Thousand and 0 Hundreds
final_answer.spoken: sixteen hundreds and one one, five thousands and sixty nine ones

maths_rules: 37,608: 17 Thousand = 17,000; 8 Ones; 37,608 − 17,008 = 20,600 = 2 Ten Thousand + 6 Hundreds
43,001: 3 Ten Thousand = 30,000; 1 One; 43,001 − 30,001 = 13,000 = 13 Thousand + 0 Hundreds
10 Hundreds = 1 Thousand; 10 Thousand = 1 Ten Thousand
